title: User accounts, groups and NTFS permissions
summary: Understand how Windows controls who can do what, from account types and groups to NTFS file permissions. By the end you can create accounts, place users in the right groups and fix 'access denied' problems.
objectives: Distinguish standard, administrator and guest account types
Explain why groups make permissions manageable at scale
Compare NTFS permissions with simpler share permissions
Apply the principle of least privilege to everyday support
Use net user and icacls to inspect and change access from the terminal
Diagnose a common 'access denied' problem and explain the cause

quiz.q: A user needs to install printer drivers but keeps getting blocked. Their account is the wrong type. Which account type can install most software and change system settings?
quiz.why: An Administrator account can install software and change system-wide settings. Standard users are deliberately limited for safety, and Guest is the most restricted of all.

quiz.q: Why do organisations assign permissions to groups rather than to individual users?
options: It is the only way Windows allows access
It scales: change one group instead of hundreds of users
quiz.why: Assigning rights to a group and then adding users to that group means you manage access in one place. When someone changes role you move them between groups instead of editing every file.

quiz.q: A file is shared on the network. The share permission allows Full Control but the NTFS permission only allows Read. What can a remote user actually do?
options: Read only — the most restrictive of the two applies
quiz.why: When share and NTFS permissions combine, the most restrictive effective permission wins. Read on NTFS caps the remote user at Read even though the share allows Full Control.

quiz.q: Which command-line tool displays and changes NTFS permissions on files and folders?
quiz.why: icacls views and modifies NTFS access control lists (ACLs). net user manages accounts, gpresult reports Group Policy, and tasklist lists processes.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is the principle of least privilege and why does it matter on a helpdesk?
quiz.answer: Give each user only the access they need to do their job and no more, so a mistake or compromised account can do the least possible damage.
quiz.why: Least privilege limits blast radius: standard users by default, elevation only when justified. It is a core security expectation in the A+ objectives.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does the command 'net user jsmith /add' do, and what should you usually do next?
quiz.answer: It creates a new local user account named jsmith; next you would set a password and add the account to the appropriate group with net localgroup.
quiz.why: net user /add creates the account, but a new account needs a password and group membership before it is genuinely useful and secure.

body_markdown:
## Who are you? Account types

Every action in Windows happens under a **user account**, and the **account type** decides what that user may do. A **standard user** can run apps and change their own settings but cannot make system-wide changes. An **administrator** can install software, change system settings and manage other accounts. The **guest** account is heavily restricted and usually disabled. The safe default for everyday work is a **standard** account; elevate only when a task truly needs it.

You can inspect and create accounts from the terminal:

```powershell
net user                       # list local accounts
net user jsmith P@ssw0rd! /add # create an account
net localgroup Administrators jsmith /add
```

## Groups: permissions that scale

Imagine setting permissions on a thousand files for fifty users — then someone leaves. Painful. Instead, Windows uses **groups**. You grant access to a **group** (say *Accounting*), then add users to that group. Change a person's role and you simply move them between groups; the files never change. Common built-in groups include **Administrators**, **Users** and **Guests**.

```cmd
net localgroup Accounting /add
net localgroup Accounting jsmith /add
```

## NTFS vs share permissions

There are two permission systems and the A+ exam loves the difference. **Share permissions** apply only when a folder is reached *over the network*. **NTFS permissions** apply *always* — locally and remotely — and are far more granular (Read, Write, Modify, Full Control, and more).

The golden rule: when both apply, the **most restrictive** effective permission wins. If the share says Full Control but NTFS says Read, a remote user gets **Read**. Because NTFS always applies, it is the system you'll tune most.

```cmd
icacls C:\Reports
C:\Reports BUILTIN\Administrators:(F)
         CONTOSO\Accounting:(M)
         BUILTIN\Users:(R)
```

The letters mean Full control (F), Modify (M), Read (R), and Write (W).

## Changing access with icacls

When a user genuinely needs more access, grant it to the right group, not the individual, and only the level required:

```cmd
icacls C:\Reports /grant CONTOSO\Accounting:(OI)(CI)M
```

The `(OI)(CI)` flags mean the permission is inherited by files and subfolders inside the folder. Always prefer Modify over Full Control unless the user must change permissions themselves.

## Least privilege and 'access denied'

The **principle of least privilege** says: give each user only the access they need, and no more. It is the single most effective everyday security habit, because a mistake or a hijacked account can then do far less harm.

Most **access denied** tickets come down to one of three things: the user is in the wrong group, an NTFS permission is too restrictive, or they didn't run a tool **as administrator**. Check group membership first (`whoami /groups`), then the folder's NTFS permissions, then elevation.

## Your task

On a test PC (or a VM), open an elevated terminal. Run `net user` to list accounts and `whoami /groups` to see your own group memberships. Create a folder `C:\Lab`, then run `icacls C:\Lab` to read its current permissions and identify which groups have Read versus Modify. Write three lines explaining who can do what, and which single group you would add to give your imaginary 'Accounting' team Modify access without touching individual users.

slides.title: Managing accounts from the terminal

slides.title: Reading NTFS with icacls
bullets: icacls shows a folder's access control list.
Letters: F full, M modify, R read, W write.
OI and CI flags mean inheritance.
NTFS always applies, so you tune it most.
slides.narration: You read and change N T F S permissions with i cackles — spelled i c a c l s. Running it on a folder lists its access control list. The letters are shorthand: F is full control, M is modify, R is read, W is write. You'll also see O I and C I flags, which mean the permission is inherited by files and subfolders. Because N T F S always applies, it's the system you'll spend the most time tuning.

slides.title: Granting access the right way
bullets: Grant to the group, never the individual.
Give only the level required.
(OI)(CI) makes it inherit into the folder.
Prefer Modify over Full Control.
slides.narration: When a user genuinely needs more access, grant it to the right group, not to the individual person, and give only the level required. Here i c a c l s slash grant gives the Accounting group Modify rights on the Reports folder, and the O I C I flags make that inherit down into files and subfolders. And notice we chose Modify, not Full Control — always prefer the lower level unless the user must change permissions themselves.

slides.title: The principle of least privilege
bullets: Give only the access the job needs, no more.
A mistake or hijacked account does less harm.
Standard accounts by default; elevate when justified.
It's a core A+ security expectation.
slides.narration: This brings us to the single most important idea in this lesson: the principle of least privilege. Give each user only the access they need to do their job, and no more. Why? Because if they make a mistake, or their account is hijacked, the damage is contained. In practice this means standard accounts by default, and elevating only when there's a clear, justified reason. It's a core security expectation in the A plus objectives.

slides.title: Tracking down 'access denied'
bullets: Cause one: user is in the wrong group.
Cause two: NTFS permission too restrictive.
Cause three: tool not run as administrator.
Check whoami /groups, then NTFS, then elevation.
slides.narration: Most access-denied tickets come down to one of three things. One: the user is in the wrong group. Two: an N T F S permission is too restrictive. Three: they simply didn't run the tool as administrator. So work it in order. First check group membership with whoami slash groups. Then look at the folder's N T F S permissions with i c a c l s. Then confirm whether elevation was needed. That sequence solves the vast majority of access problems.
